children.text: Tutankhamun's tomb isn't the largest in the
Valley of the Kings
. Nor the most magnificently decorated. The small tomb known as KV62 played a decisive role in showing ancient Egypt to the world.

When Howard Carter found this tomb in 1922, many Valley of the Kings tombs were already looted in antiquity. Tutankhamun's tomb still held the king's grave goods in great quantity. Golden mask, coffins, shrines, chariots, throne, jewellery, daily goods, ritual items. The discovery shocked not only archaeology but 20th-century popular culture.
Tutankhamun himself wasn't a long-reigning powerful king. His fame was born less from lifetime achievements and more from the tomb surviving nearly intact. The chance is what makes this tomb special.
The Valley of the Kings and hidden tombs
The Valley of the Kings is in a dry valley on
Luxor
's west bank. New Kingdom kings chose hiding tombs in mountains over conspicuous pyramids — to deter looting.
Many hidden tombs were still looted in antiquity. Even with sealed entrances, interior treasures were taken in many cases. Priests later moved royal mummies elsewhere for protection.
Among those, Tutankhamun's tomb being found with much grave goods was very rare. Traces of ancient intrusion exist; not fully emptied.
Howard Carter's discovery
Howard Carter was a British archaeologist long active in Egypt. He believed Tutankhamun's tomb remained somewhere in the Valley of the Kings and continued excavation with Lord Carnarvon's support.
In November 1922, workers found stone steps. Beyond was a sealed entrance, with another blocked entrance further in. When Carter peered through a small hole, gold-shining items appeared.

The moment is told as a symbolic scene in archaeological history. The actual excavation and recording proceeded over long time. Rather than rushing items out, Carter's team carefully photographed, recorded, preserved, and moved.
The tomb's structure
KV62 is small as royal tombs go. Main spaces — antechamber, annex, burial chamber, treasury. Compared with nearby Ramesside large tombs, both passages and rooms are modest.
The smallness ties to Tutankhamun dying young and burial possibly prepared in haste. A tomb originally for another person possibly used for the king is also pointed out.

Decoration is mainly in the burial chamber. Walls depict Tutankhamun heading to the afterworld and the opening-of-the-mouth ritual. Less decoration than other large tombs; with a tension of being arranged hastily for a young king's burial.
What was in the tomb
Thousands of items were found in Tutankhamun's tomb. The golden mask is most famous; only part of the whole.

The antechamber held animal-shaped beds, chariots, boxes, furniture, vessels, and daily goods. The treasury held canopic chest, divine images, model boats, and ritual items. The burial chamber held nested shrines, sarcophagus, multiple coffins, and the king's mummy.

These items aren't only treasures. Things deemed needed for the king to continue living in the afterworld. Food, clothes, weapons, furniture, amulets, statues, and ritual gear were placed to support the king heading to the afterlife.
Looking at tomb contents, you see ancient Egyptian royal burial wasn't only golden lavishness but concrete preparation for the afterworld.
Why the golden mask became famous

Tutankhamun's golden mask is one of the most famous items symbolising ancient Egypt. The idealised young king's face, blue-and-gold stripes, and decoration showing sacred kingship leave strong impression.
The mask wasn't made as art to be shown to people. A funerary tool to protect the king's mummy and help transformation in the afterworld.

In modern times, through photos and exhibitions, the mask became widely known and, more than Tutankhamun himself, became the image of ancient Egypt itself. A king unremarkable in life became a global symbol through burial goods.
Why the tomb survived
The reasons Tutankhamun's tomb survived relatively well aren't one. The tomb being small and the entrance covered by debris from later work may have delayed discovery.

Tutankhamun is also a king tied to the Amarna-era chaos, with later kings tending to erase his name from records. Ironically, being forgotten diverted attention from those who sought tombs and contributed to preservation.
Not a completely undisturbed tomb. Traces of ancient intrusion exist. With many Valley of the Kings tombs nearly empty, this much grave goods remaining together made the discovery's value decisive.
What kind of king was Tutankhamun
Tutankhamun likely took the throne around age 9 and ruled about ten years. His era was when traditional god worship was restored after Akhenaten's religious reform.
As a young king, actual political judgments were likely greatly influenced by powerful figures and bureaucrats around him. How far he himself led policy needs careful thinking.

Causes of his death — illness, fractures, infection, genetic health issues — are debated. Assassination has been spoken of; no decisive evidence today. For travellers, holding that he died young, and that hastier burial likely followed, is enough.
Where the items are now
Most Tutankhamun grave goods were long displayed and stored at the old Egyptian Museum in
Cairo
. Now, Tutankhamun-related material can be seen at the Grand Egyptian Museum.
As of May 2026, official ticket information includes Tutankhamun Galleries in GEM visit range. Display range and entry conditions may change; confirm official information before visiting.
KV62 in the Valley of the Kings holds the sarcophagus, coffins, and the king's mummy. So to understand Tutankhamun, seeing both the Luxor tomb and the
Giza
museum makes it more three-dimensional.
Visiting KV62 today
Tutankhamun's tomb may need a supplementary ticket in the Valley of the Kings. Ticket handling, opening status, and photo rules change; confirm on-site.
Before visiting, know KV62 is small, not the most visually magnificent. For decorative richness in the Valley of the Kings, Ramesses V/VI or Seti I tombs leave stronger impressions.
KV62 holds meaning others don't. The place Carter found in 1922 and where the young king's mummy long lay.
When entering, see it as the discovery site, not expecting golden items. Small burial chamber, wall paintings, sarcophagus, mummy. They sit at the centre of a discovery that moved the world.
See as discovery story, not curse
Tutankhamun's tomb ties strongly to "the pharaoh's curse." From Lord Carnarvon's death, newspapers and popular culture spread the story.

For understanding KV62, what really matters isn't the curse. What matters is a tomb in the Valley of the Kings with this many grave goods being found, and the discovery greatly changing world interest in ancient Egypt.

The curse is part of the tomb's modern reception. To see the tomb itself, looking at the young king's burial, afterworld preparation, and the meaning of items surviving more than three thousand years gives a far deeper experience.
Tutankhamun's tomb isn't the most lavishly decorated. Not the largest. In showing a nearly lost royal-tomb world in collected form to the present, it is irreplaceable.

Without this tomb, we would understand New Kingdom royal burial far more fragmentarily. Beyond the golden mask — boxes, staves, clothes, food, boats, amulets, small daily items — the whole tomb was made to support the king's afterworld.

When visiting KV62, no need to be disappointed by the small scale. That small space made Tutankhamun the world's most famous pharaoh. The tomb teaches not the king's greatness but the power of preserved chance.
